---
title: "The Silicon Sample Benchmark: A multi-team preregistration for predicting behavioral-experiment effects"

abstract: |
    This is the preregistration for the **Silicon Sample Benchmark**, a multi-team prediction benchmark. We invite independent research teams to predict the results of a novel behavioral megastudy (16 message interventions to increase trust in climate scientists, 13 preregistered outcomes, a representative U.S. sample of ~18,000) with any AI-based approach they choose, from behavioral clones to group-level simulation to direct effect forecasting. At the time of writing, human data collection is complete (~18,000 responses). None of these data have been shared, published, or made accessible to any prospective team, and no team will be granted access before the prediction lock. Before any human data are released, every team registers its predictions using a standardized method-registration form (an extended version of the GUIDE-LLM reporting checklist) and deposits its predictions on Zenodo.

```{.r .cell-code}
# packages
library(tidyverse)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(broom)
library(MetBrewer)
library(gghalves)
library(patchwork)
library(gt)
library(tinytable)
library(here)

# custom functions (reused unchanged from the original preregistration)
source(here("R/functions/statistics.R"))
source(here("R/functions/plots.R"))
source(here("R/functions/tables.R"))
source(here("R/functions/reporting.R"))

# simulated (random) placeholder data
human_data     <- readRDS(here("data/simulation_preregistration/human_data_preregistration.rds"))
llm_data_teams <- readRDS(here("data/simulation_preregistration/llm_data_preregistration_teams.rds"))

# Restrict the human data to the scored conditions (the 16 non-interactive
# interventions + control) BEFORE any model is fit. The real cleaned human
# data will additionally contain the three chatbot arms and the value-
# similarity arm, which no submission predicts; fitting the human models on
# those arms would put the human side's BH adjustment over a different test
# family than the submissions'.
#
# The scored set comes from the canonical intervention list
# (data/interventions.csv, titles trimmed, the four interactive arms
# excluded) — never from a submission's own condition labels, so a mislabeled
# or missing condition in a submission can neither widen nor shrink the
# scoring universe. The placeholder simulation uses generic intervention_N
# labels that are not in the canonical list; there the scored set falls back
# to the conditions the simulation generates (all scorable by construction),
# which keeps this document renderable. With real submissions the canonical
# path binds.
canonical_interventions <- read_csv(here("data/interventions.csv"),
                                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(str_trim(tag) != "LLM-chatbot", str_trim(title) != "Value similarity") |>
  pull(title) |> str_trim() |> unique()

scored_conditions <- if (any(canonical_interventions %in%
                             unique(as.character(llm_data_teams$condition)))) {
  c("control", canonical_interventions)
} else {
  levels(droplevels(factor(llm_data_teams$condition)))
}

human_data <- human_data |>
  filter(condition %in% scored_conditions) |>
  mutate(condition = droplevels(condition))

# Same preregistered random split of the human sample as in the original
# preregistration. Human 1 is the reference half all submissions are scored
# against; Human 2 is the human replication reference.
set.seed(42)
split_ids    <- sample(unique(human_data$id), size = floor(length(unique(human_data$id)) / 2))
human_data_1 <- human_data |> filter(id %in% split_ids)
human_data_2 <- human_data |> filter(!id %in% split_ids)
```

**This is the canonical preregistration for the benchmark.** It is self-contained. The full analysis plan is restated here (see *Analysis plan*), so a participating team does not need to open the project's earlier single-team preregistration ([v1](preregistration.qmd)). The section *About this preregistration* explains why this second preregistration exists, what it keeps from v1, and every way it changes.

The benchmark's public-facing design (motivation, rules, the three tiers, the full method-registration form, the disclosure policy, scoring, and the timeline) is also described in the [call for participation](index.html). To avoid duplication, this document summarizes that design only as far as the analysis needs it, and concentrates on the analysis plan. Where the two overlap, the call is the canonical description of the procedure and this document is the canonical description of the analysis.

All datasets used for demonstration here are simulated random noise with the correct structure.
:::

## Motivation

Whether large language models (LLMs) can predict how human participants behave in surveys and experiments is a consequential open question in social sciences. The evidence so far is mixed, and has methodological issues: Most existing evaluations target experiments that were already published, and plausibly in the models’ training data. Even in cases where the data from these published experiments is outside of the LLMs' training data, reported success rates may still be biased by researcher degrees of freedom. The analytical procedure, evaluation metrics, models, and prompts researchers use impact their findings considerably [@cumminsThreatAnalyticFlexibility2025b]. A credible evaluation of LLMs' potential for predicting human behavior in social science research requires new data and preregistered methods. 

To address these issues, we aim to provide a preregistered, multi-team prediction benchmark, the *Silicon Sample Benchmark*. Independent teams predict the same novel megastudy (N ≈ 18,000) with any AI-based approach, and all approaches are evaluated using the same preregistered procedures. The target data is novel, and none of the interventions has been tested in their exact form before. All teams' predictions are deposited and time-stamped before any human data are released. The full rationale, rules, and incentives for participating teams are laid out in the [call for participation](index.html).

The benchmark scores the 16 non-interactive text interventions of the megastudy^[The original experiment contains 20 intervention conditions plus a shared control. The benchmark scores only the 16 non-interactive text interventions. The four left out are the three interactive LLM-chatbot arms and the "Value similarity" quiz, all of which depend on a live back-and-forth that would substantially complicate the simulation task.], across self-reported attitudes (e.g., trust in climate scientists, support for funding of climate science) and behavioral measures (a donation to a scientific organization, a newsletter sign-up).

The goal of the benchmark is *not* to crown a single champion team. Instead, we aim to map the current design space of synthetic sample approaches and to evaluate, as a field, how well they predict human behavior. This benchmark study will provide a catalogue---a structured, comparable description of how research teams currently approach AI prediction of behavioral experiments (open- vs. closed-weight models, persona sources, administration protocols, fine-tuning, in-context learning). We will evaluate approaches on a set of metrics, from directional agreement to calibration, plus distributional fidelity and stereotyping diagnostics (all specified in full under *Analysis plan*, below). We expect different approaches to win on different metrics.

@tbl-interventions gives an overview of the 16 interventions, grouped by their content. All are short text messages (e.g., an article, an interview excerpt, corrected statistics, a portrait) shown once before the outcome battery. Together with the shared control condition they make up the 17 conditions every submission needs to cover.


::: {#tbl-interventions .cell tbl-cap='The 16 text-based interventions scored in the benchmark, grouped by the broad angle each takes on trust in climate scientists. The **Code name** column gives the internal condition identifier used in the raw survey files (`survey.qsf` / `survey.json`) in the submission template. Each intervention has exactly one code name; where intervention-author teams were combined, the code name is a semicolon-joined list, and the semicolons are part of the name (see `survey/condition_codenames.csv` in the benchmark repository). The original megastudy also fields three interactive LLM-chatbot arms and a \'Value similarity\' quiz; these four interventions are interactive and excluded from the simulation benchmark, leaving 16 interventions plus a shared control condition (17 conditions in total).'}

```{.r .cell-code}
interventions <- read_csv(here("data/interventions.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

tag_order <- c(
  "Collaboration and peer-review",
  "Scientific methods and results",
  "Applications and impact",
  "Others' endorsement",
  "Values",
  "Other"
)

# Same table layout as v1: category headers inserted
# as bold full-width rows, with a running intervention number.
intervention_table_data <- interventions |>
  mutate(across(c(title, summary, tag, code_name), str_trim)) |>
  filter(tag != "LLM-chatbot", title != "Value similarity") |>
  mutate(tag = factor(tag, levels = tag_order)) |>
  arrange(tag, title) |>
  mutate(number = as.character(row_number())) |>
  # internal condition code names exactly as in the raw survey files
  # (survey.qsf / survey.json); semicolon-joined names are a
  # single identifier — semicolons are part of the name, never split.
  mutate(codename = code_name) |>
  group_by(tag) |>
  group_modify(~ bind_rows(
    tibble(title = as.character(.y$tag), codename = "", summary = ""),
    .x
  )) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(` ` = ifelse(title %in% levels(tag), "", number)) |>
  select(` `, title, codename, summary) |>
  rename(`Intervention Title` = title, `Code name` = codename, Summary = summary)

# identify header rows
header_rows <- which(intervention_table_data$` ` == "")

intervention_table_data |>
  tt(width = c(0.04, 0.19, 0.17, 0.60)) |>
  format_tt(escape = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(align = "l", alignv = "t") |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(i = header_rows, bold = TRUE, j = 2, colspan = 3) |>
  style_tt(j = 3, monospace = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.85)
```

@tbl-outcomes summarizes the 13 preregistered outcomes every submission predicts: the primary trust composite, ten further attitude measures (all 0–100 sliders), and two behavioral measures. Multi-item scales enter the analysis as the mean of their items. The exact item wordings and response scales are provided in a codebook in the [submission template repository](https://github.com/janpfander/silicon-sample-submission).

## About this preregistration

**Why a second preregistration.** The project began as a single-team simulation study, preregistered as *"Predicting the effects of behavioral interventions on humans with LLMs"* (the original preregistration, **v1**). That plan asked how well one approach, an individual-level simulation built by members of the core team from demographically representative U.S. profiles with one particular model and prompt, recovers a novel megastudy. But a single team's result is only one point in a large space of ways to build a synthetic sample. We therefore decided to turn the project into a **multi-team benchmark** in which many independent teams predict the same novel experiment with any AI-based approach, and every approach is scored identically. This new preregistration plan supersedes the original **v1** preregistration.

**What it keeps from v1.** The human target study and the estimands (average treatment effects per intervention × outcome, subgroup interactions, control-condition response distributions, and demographic baselines), the three-section analysis structure, the least-to-most-strict ordering of the comparison metrics, and the preregistered split-half **human replication reference** are all carried over from v1. All are restated below (see *Analysis plan*) to keep this new preregistration self-contained. The model functions are reused unchanged.

**What it changes and adds.** The changes fall into four groups. Group A redesigns the study, group B changes what it reports, group C adds scoring tools from the recent silicon-sample literature, and group D collects the revisions made after an external methods review of this document. Each change is summarized here, with a pointer to the section that specifies it in full.

Because this preregistration is written for teams who are blinded to the human outcome data, revising the analysis plan does not carry the usual risk of data-contingent researcher degrees of freedom.

**A. From one approach to a field.** These change the *design*, leaving v1's analysis pipeline untouched.

1. **Single team → multi-team benchmark.** The project now evaluates a *field* of independent submissions rather than one core-team approach. It allows for submissions at different levels (Tier 1 individual-level synthetic data, Tier 2 cell-level statistics, Tier 3 effect-level estimates). See *Benchmark design*.
2. **Method registration and disclosure.** Every team documents its pipeline on a standardized method-registration form (an extended GUIDE-LLM checklist) and deposits its predictions under a disclosure policy that keeps even proprietary entries verifiable. See *Method registration and disclosure*.
3. **Per-tier submission specifications.** Each tier has an exact file schema, and each tier's file is reduced to the same set of effect estimates before scoring, so predictions are comparable across tiers. See *Submission specification*.

**B. Additional benchmark design choices.** Benchmark specific results are mere add-ons to the original v1 pipeline. No estimand or model inherited from v1 is redefined.

4. **The headline result is the field, not a single scorecard.** The primary result is no longer one approach's report card but the distribution of predictive quality across the whole field of approaches. Every approach is scored against a split-half **human replication reference** (how well one half of the human sample predicts the other). Teams may enter more than once, capped at three entries per tier, and every entry appears in all main analyses (item 16). Every entry must cover the full study (all 16 interventions × 13 outcomes), so all scores are measured on the same basis. See *Cross-team comparison*.
5. **One score per metric, pooled across outcomes.** A single data point is one predicted effect placed next to the matching human effect, for example how much a particular message shifted trust in climate scientists. We deliberately do *not* collapse the metrics into one overall "champion" score. An approach can get the direction of effects right while mis-scaling their size, or do well on the main outcome and badly on the rest, and a single number would hide exactly the structure the benchmark exists to reveal. Each metric is therefore read on its own. See *Cross-team comparison* (*Scoring principle*). That said, in our main figures, we will report correlations (and adjusted correlations).
6. **An uncertainty interval on every score.** The benchmark tests 16 interventions, but these are only a sample of all possible kinds of messages one could have tested. A different study could have used 16 other messages. An approach's score is therefore an estimate, and like any estimate it would move somewhat under a different draw of interventions. With bootstrap sampling, we attach an interval to every score showing how much it might move based on message selection. For the same reason, we never call one approach better than another from the ranking alone. See *Uncertainty intervals on the leaderboard*.
7. **Point predictions only.** v1's comparison metrics included inferential agreement (does the prediction reach the same significance verdict as the human data?) and an equivalence test, both of which need an uncertainty around each predicted effect. In the benchmark, teams submit point predictions without uncertainty intervals, and these two metrics are not part of the cross-team scoring. Submitted intervals would have created their own problems: a team could make every prediction "not significant" simply by submitting wide intervals, which in a world of mostly small effects scores well without skill, and closing that loophole would have required extra interval-scoring metrics and cross-tier standardizations of no substantive interest. The remaining metrics (direction, rank and linear correlation, absolute error, calibration) capture predictive quality without any submitted uncertainty. See *Comparison functions* and *Cross-team comparison*.

**C. New evaluation add-ons from the silicon-sample literature.** The remaining additions extend the originally proposed evaluation metrics from v1. The new metrics are motivated by how recent studies have evaluated synthetic samples. They supplement or improve the inherited metrics from v1.

8. **A noise-corrected correlation.** The human effects an approach is scored against are estimated from a (here, half-split) sample which is not perfectly representing the population.
The resulting sampling noise can drag down the correlations between human and synthetic sample effects. Because the sampling noise is unrelated to predictive skill, we try to account for it. Following @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a, we report a noise-corrected correlation beside the raw one (the raw value stays the ranked metric). See *Comparison functions*.
9. **A floor for the metrics without a natural zero.** RMSE has no natural zero to read it against. Adding a naive "predict no effect for everything" approach as a floor reference makes such scores more interpretable. Each approach can then be interpreted by its distance to that floor, and to the human reference [@ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a; @cumminsThreatAnalyticFlexibility2025b]. See *Comparison functions*.
10. **Subgroup distributions.** Averaging outcome distributions over demographic groups can hide an approach that serves most groups well but consistently misses one. We report the gap between the worst- and best-served group in terms of distribution similarity [@parkLLMAgentsGrounded2026]. Because too-similar synthetic responses (under-dispersion) are the problem the literature flags most often, we make under-dispersion the headline distribution diagnostic. See *Section 3*, and *Section 1* (response distributions).
11. **Human sample split robustness.** The human sample is divided in half at random to build the reference. That split is fixed before any data are seen, so it is not a researcher degree of freedom. But the particular split we drew is still arbitrary, and another random split would serve just as well. To show the results do not hinge on the one we happened to draw, we recompute them across many alternative splits and report how stable they are [@cumminsThreatAnalyticFlexibility2025b]. See *Cross-team comparison*.
12. **One unit for all outcomes.** The outcome measures use different scales, with 0–100 attitude sliders, a $0–10 donation, and a 0–1 signup probability. To make effects on these scales comparable, we convert them to **percentage points of its outcome's scale range** before any cross-outcome scoring, following the practice of @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a. The binary newsletter outcome is added to the subgroup analysis on the same footing, via the linear probability model. See *Cross-team comparison* (*Scoring principle*) and *Section 2*.
13. **A pooled calibration regression.** v1 runs the calibration regression per outcome, on 16 points each. The benchmark instead pools all condition × outcome pairs into one regression (16 × 13 = 208 points, in percentage points of scale range), the same way @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a estimate their calibration slope across all effects of an archive. See *Comparison functions* (*Calibration regression*).
14. **A fourth distribution metric.** Beside v1's variance ratio, OVL, and KS, the response-distribution analyses add the Wasserstein-1 distance (W1), a bandwidth-free companion to the KDE-based OVL. See *Comparison functions* (*Distribution comparison metrics*).
15. **Calibration reported descriptively.** v1 tested calibration with two F-tests (the joint α = 0, β = 1 and the slope-only β = 1) and reported the regression's R². The benchmark drops the tests and the R², and reports α and β with 95% CIs, read descriptively. Four reasons. At this reference precision (roughly 18,000 humans behind 208 points), every realistic approach rejects exact calibration, so the tests do not separate approaches. The tests also treat the 208 pooled points as independent, although the 13 outcomes within an intervention share that intervention's draw and all points share one control arm, so their p-values are overconfident. The precedent we follow, @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a, reports the slope with a CI and interprets its size, and keeping α alongside it is what their advice to linearly recalibrate predictions needs. And dropping the tests is consistent with removing the other significance-test metrics (item 7). The calibration R² goes because it equals the squared pooled Pearson r already on the leaderboard. The 95% intervals for α and β come from the same intervention cluster bootstrap as every other metric, which respects the dependence just described, where heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors would not (item 18). See *Comparison functions* (*Calibration regression*).
16. **A cap of three entries per tier, and every entry enters the main analyses.** Each team may submit up to three entries per tier (so up to nine in total). Where a team has good reasons to systematically vary some aspect of an approach, we may grant additional entries on request, but only three per tier enter the main analyses. All of a team's entries appear in every analysis, including the field summary (Finding 1) and the leaderboard (Finding 2). Scoring every entry gives the benchmark more approaches and more variation between approaches, and the per-tier cap limits how much any single team can shape the field distribution. Each team still designates exactly one of its entries, across all tiers, as its **primary entry** before the prediction lock. As a robustness analysis, the main results are recomputed on primary entries only, a field with exactly one entry per team (see *Cross-team comparison*, *Primaries-only robustness*). In the figures and the leaderboard, entries appear under neutral labels (`submission_1` for a single-entry team, `submission_2_a`, `submission_2_b`, … for a multi-entry team, with `_a` the primary). An appendix table maps each label to its team.

**D. Revisions after external review.** Before registration, a member of the core team reviewed this document in detail. The following revisions came out of that review (together with wording clarifications throughout). All were made before any submission was received, and none was informed by human outcome data.

17. **A noise-corrected calibration slope for Tier 1.** Sampling noise in the *predicted* effects drags the calibration slope toward zero (noise in the human reference never does — it only widens the residuals), so a noisy but well-calibrated submission prints β < 1 without exaggerating anything, and by an amount that depends on its synthetic sample size. Because Tier-1 effects are refit by us, their standard errors are known, and we report a corrected slope beside the raw one: raw β divided by the reliability of the predicted effects. The raw β stays the Ashokkumar-comparable quantity. Tiers 2–3 submit no uncertainty, so no correction exists there and the wording carries the caveat. See *Comparison functions* (*Calibration regression*).
18. **Cluster-bootstrap calibration intervals.** The α and β intervals now come from the intervention cluster bootstrap (same seed and draws as every other metric) instead of heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, which treated the 208 pooled points as independent — a dependence this document itself flags in item 15. See *Comparison functions* (*Calibration regression*).
19. **An empirical chance level for directional agreement.** Every intervention was designed to *increase* trust, so if most human effects come out positive, a mindless "every message works" strategy beats 50% without skill. An all-positive baseline row is added beside the no-effect floor, and its directional score — the share of positive human ATEs — is the chance level to read the field against. Predicted exact zeros score half credit: a zero makes no directional claim, so it earns what a coin flip earns, and the no-effect floor accordingly reads 50%. See *Cross-team comparison*.
20. **Adjusted RMSE reported as 0 at the reference noise.** When a submission's errors are smaller than the sampling noise of the human reference estimates, the noise-corrected RMSE used to come out undefined (NA) — punishing exactly the best submissions and dropping their best bootstrap replicates. It is now reported as 0 with a flag: indistinguishable from perfect at this reference precision. See *Comparison functions*.
21. **A within-outcome companion correlation.** The pooled Pearson r credits two different kinds of knowledge: which *outcomes* are movable at all (generic knowledge, available from the literature) and which *messages* work (the skill this benchmark tests). We additionally report the correlation computed within outcomes (each outcome's mean effect subtracted on both sides, the outcome-fixed-effects estimate). What survives is message-level skill only, and the gap to the pooled r says how much of the field's headline number came from outcome knowledge. See *Cross-team comparison*.
22. **A secondary self-report vs. behavioral cut.** The two behavioral outcomes contribute 32 of the 208 pooled pairs, so the pooled metrics cannot say whether an approach that predicts stated attitudes also predicts what people do. The pooled metrics are recomputed within the eleven self-report outcomes and within the two behavioral outcomes, registered as a designated secondary result. See *Cross-team comparison* (*Where the field predicts well*).
23. **Baseline calibration without correlations.** Section 3a used to report a Pearson correlation over each moderator's group means. Those correlations run over three to seven points — over two points a correlation is always exactly ±1 — and correlation ignores level and scale, the two things baseline calibration is about. The section now rests on the RMSE of the group means, the demographic parity gap, and the per-group display. See *Section 3*.
24. **Stereotyping read from the group gaps.** A higher demographic R² in a synthetic sample than in humans can mean two things: the group differences are exaggerated, or the synthetic individuals answer too much alike, which shrinks the residual variance and inflates R² even when every group mean is right. The regression's group coefficients — the predicted group gaps next to the human ones — become the primary stereotyping quantity, and the R² comparison stays as the demographic-predictability summary with that two-source reading stated. Under-dispersion is diagnosed separately by the variance ratio. See *Section 3*.
25. **Visible minimum-group-size exclusions.** Groups under 30 respondents on either side were silently skipped in the demographic parity gap, and the smallest groups are exactly the metric's motivating population. Skipped groups are now named, with their sizes, wherever the parity gap is reported. The within-subgroup distribution comparisons, which had no minimum at all, apply the same threshold. See *Section 2* and *Section 3*.
26. **A fixed grid for the distribution metrics.** The overlap coefficient and the Wasserstein-1 distance used to be computed over the observed minimum-to-maximum range of each human–submission pair, so every submission was scored on a slightly different grid. The grid is now fixed to each outcome's full scale range (0–100 for the sliders, $0–10 for the donation), identical for every submission. See *Comparison functions* (*Distribution comparison metrics*).
27. **The Tier-2 moderator file must be complete.** The file schema used to allow NA for moderator cells an approach "cannot" produce. But every Tier-2 team already predicts each condition mean in its main file, and repeating that mean in a group's cells is an honest, always-available prediction of "no moderation for this group" — so NA really meant "I'd rather not be scored here", and pairwise exclusion would have scored different teams on different, self-chosen cell sets. The validator now rejects NAs, and the repeat-the-condition-mean convention is documented in the submission template. See *Submission specification*.
28. **Weighting scope written down.** If the megastudy's preregistered attrition checks trigger inverse-probability weighting, the weights apply to *all* human-side mean and regression estimates that enter scoring — the ATEs, the interaction estimates, and the demographic group means, in both human halves. The distribution comparisons are the stated exception and stay unweighted. Deciding this now closes a fork that would otherwise have been resolved after seeing data. See *The human target sample*.
29. **A hardened scoring pipeline.** The set of scored conditions is derived from the canonical intervention list, never from a submission's own labels, and every pair-building join asserts the full intervention × outcome grid with no missing estimates — a submission that cannot be paired completely stops the pipeline instead of being silently scored on the surviving subset. See *Cross-team comparison*.
30. **The core team does not submit.** No member of the core team enters the benchmark, and the passage that reserved that option is removed.

## The human target sample

Synthetic sample predictions are scored against the human data from the megastudy. Participants are recruited from a non-probability opt-in panel, quota-matched (age, gender and race) to the population of U.S. residents, all aged 18 or older, who pass a series of attention and bot-detection checks before treatment assignment.

The benchmark targets **N ≈ 18,000 complete responses**, with 1,000 per intervention across the 16 text-based interventions plus 2,000 in the shared control condition. Recruitment uses **census-based cross quotas** on gender × age and gender × race/ethnicity to approximate the U.S. adult population. The targets below match the proportions of the parent megastudy, with counts rescaled to a total N ≈ 18,000. Participants selecting "Other" as their gender are not quota-constrained.

The targets below are drawn from the 2024 U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates Program. *Total* is the share within each category. *Male* and *Female* give the within-category gender split. The table describes the key demographics of the human sample. Participating teams are not required to use this information for their own synthetic sample.

Full sampling and exclusion detail is in the [human study preregistration](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20160212). The human reference estimates follow that preregistration's analysis plan throughout; in particular, its preregistered checks for differential attrition may lead the human models to apply inverse-probability weights, in which case submissions are scored against the weighted estimates. If that happens, the weights apply to **all** human-side mean and regression estimates that enter scoring — the ATEs, the condition × moderator interaction estimates, and the demographic group means, in both human halves — so no analysis scores an unweighted human quantity against a weighted one. The response-distribution comparisons are the one stated exception and stay unweighted: they compare raw respondent-level distributions, and reweighted density estimation would introduce machinery of its own with no counterpart in the human study's plan.

## Benchmark design

Participation is by invitation. Each team builds an AI-based prediction pipeline from the shipped materials, including intervention texts, the full survey instrument, the codebook, and the registration template.

Teams can use any models, personas, prompts, fine-tuning, retrieval, or prior data and literature they want. Before the prediction lock deadline, each team registers its approach by depositing its synthetic sample/predictions and materials on Zenodo, hashed and time-stamped. After the prediction lock deadline, every submission runs through the preregistered analysis pipeline unchanged and is reported on a public leaderboard alongside the human replication reference, and in a joint manuscript with all participating teams as co-authors. There are three ground rules for an entry to be valid: **No data access.** By design, no participating team has access to the human data. **Pipelines are AI-based and automated.** Predictions may be made based on previously published human data, but no new human data specific to this project may be collected. **Everything is registered** (see the disclosure policy below). The full procedure, ground rules, timeline, and incentives are in the [call for participation](index.html).

**Blinding and data access.** The collected human data (all ~18,000 responses; collection complete at the time of writing) have been accessed only by the research lead, Jan Pfänder, for data-quality monitoring and for the preliminary interim results presented at the talks disclosed below. No member of the core team enters the benchmark.

For full disclosure, Jan Pfänder presented some very preliminary results (human megastudy sample at the time N ≈ 3000) from an initial simulation attempt (following preregistration **v1**) in a five-minute talk at a closed academic workshop at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin (May 2026). This is the only presentation that has targeted an audience of potential collaborators on the benchmark study. It focused on the prediction ability of the simulation approach and revealed nothing about how humans behaved in the megastudy. Two other talks were explicitly about the human megastudy results. Jan Pfänder presented preliminary results from the human megastudy at an invited talk at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin (May 2026, N at the time ≈ 3000 of 22000), and at a small conference at the University of Hohenheim (June 2026, N at the time ≈ 13000 of 22000). No one in the audience of these talks will be invited to participate in the benchmark study. In addition, since we ask for extensive disclosure of materials, a "cheating" prompt (e.g., "make sure intervention XX does best") would surface in the reporting framework that teams are required to fill out.

### Three ways to compete

Submissions enter at one of **three tiers**, defined by the granularity of the prediction. Teams choose the highest tier their approach supports. Lower tiers are simply eligible for fewer analyses.

- **Tier 1 · Individual-level synthetic data.** Eligible for everything, meaning ATE recovery, calibration regression, response distributions, subgroup heterogeneity, demographic baselines, and stereotyping diagnostics. *Grain: 1 row = 1 synthetic respondent.*
- **Tier 2 · Group-level treatment effect predictions.** Eligible for ATEs, calibration, subgroup heterogeneity, and demographic baselines. Not eligible for the distribution-shape metrics (variance ratio, OVL, KS, W1) or the predictability regressions. *Grain: 1 row = 1 cell (condition × [moderator level ×] outcome).*
- **Tier 3 · Average treatment effect predictions.** Eligible for ATE recovery and the calibration regression. *Grain: 1 row = 1 intervention × outcome estimate.*

### Analysis eligibility by tier

| Preregistered analysis | Tier 1 | Tier 2 | Tier 3 |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| ATE recovery (Section 1) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Calibration regression $\alpha$ / $\beta$ (Section 1) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Response distributions, variance ratio, OVL, KS, W1 (Section 1) | ✓ | — | — |
| Subgroup heterogeneity, condition × moderator (Section 2) | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| Within-subgroup distributions (Section 2) | ✓ | — | — |
| Demographic baseline calibration (Section 3) | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| Demographic predictability / stereotyping (Section 3) | ✓ | — | — |

## Method registration and disclosure

Before the prediction lock, every team documents its pipeline on a structured **method-registration form** and deposits it alongside the predictions. The form builds on the GUIDE-LLM reporting checklist [@feuerriegelReportingChecklistLarge2026]. The form and the **disclosure policy** (which lets proprietary teams seal items under escrow while keeping the lock publicly verifiable) are published in the [call for participation](index.html#registration-form). We provide a template in the [benchmark submission template repository](https://github.com/janpfander/silicon-sample-submission). 

## Submission specification

The deposit logistics (Zenodo record structure, the `metadata.json` file, file naming, the self-check validator, and the public/escrowed split) are specified in the [call for participation](index.html) and the [benchmark submission template repository](https://github.com/janpfander/silicon-sample-submission). This section only specifies aspects that matter for the analysis. Column labels and factor levels must match the published codebook (`codebook.csv`) exactly; condition labels must match the intervention titles in `survey/condition_codenames.csv` and the example prediction files exactly, with the control condition written as lowercase `control`. Every submission must cover all 16 interventions and all 13 outcomes (see *Cross-team comparison*).

### Tier 1 — individual-level dataset

One row per synthetic respondent, with the columns listed below (an example file ships in the submission template repository). Each team supplies its own synthetic respondents. `profile_id` is a team-assigned identifier, unique within the submission, and assignment of respondents to conditions (between-subjects, covering all 17 conditions) is the team's responsibility, registered under form items D.1 and D.3.

| Column(s) | Type | Specification |
|---|---|------|
| `profile_id` | string | A unique respondent identifier you assign (unique within the submission). |
| `condition` | factor | `control` (lowercase) or one of the 16 intervention titles, exactly as in `survey/condition_codenames.csv`. |
| `gender`, `age_band`, `race`, `education`, `income`, `party` | factor | The six moderators, levels per codebook (from your own profiles). |
| `trust_multidimensional` + 12 trust items | numeric | Primary composite 0–100. The 12 underlying items per codebook scale. |
| `trust_post`, `distrust_post`, `funding_perceptions`, `policy_role_mean`, `inst_trust_mean` | numeric | Secondary outcomes, original scales per codebook. |
| `belief_post`, `concern_mean`, `policy_general`, `policy_specific_mean`, `behavior_mean` | numeric | Tertiary outcomes, original scales per codebook. |
| `donation_ams` | numeric | Donation to AMS in $, per codebook. |
| `newsletter_signup` | 0 / 1 | Binary behavioral outcome. |

Because a Tier 1 submission has the same shape as the human participant data, the same analysis code applies. 

**Precision requirement.** An approach's estimated effects are only as precise as the synthetic sample behind them. The fewer synthetic respondents, the noisier each estimated effect, and a very small sample would score poorly for a reason that has nothing to do with the method. A Tier 1 submission must therefore contain at least as many synthetic respondents as the human half it is scored against, meaning **500 per intervention and 1,000 in the control condition**. At that size the submission's effects carry about the same sampling noise as the human reference. We encourage teams to go well beyond this minimum. A larger synthetic sample gives more precise effect estimates that reflect the method rather than the luck of a particular draw, and synthetic respondents are relatively cheap to generate.

### Tier 2 — cell-level file(s)

Two long-format files. `*_cells_main.csv` has one row per condition × outcome, and `*_cells_moderator.csv` one row per condition × moderator × moderator-level × outcome. Overall ATEs are derived from the main file (treatment minus control cell mean) and subgroup estimates from the moderator file, so no separate effect-level file is needed.

| Column | Type | Specification |
|---|---|------|
| `condition` | factor | Per `survey/condition_codenames.csv` (lowercase `control`). |
| `moderator`, `moderator_level` | factor | Moderator file only. Levels per codebook. |
| `outcome` | string | Outcome variable name per codebook. |
| `mean` | numeric | Predicted cell mean on the original scale (proportion for `newsletter_signup`). Both files must be complete, with no `NA` cells. To predict *no moderation* for a demographic group, repeat the condition mean from the main file in that group's cells — an always-available, honest prediction that the intervention works the same for that group (changelog item 27). The validator rejects files with missing cells. |

### Tier 3 — effect-level file

One row per intervention × outcome (16 × 13 = 208 rows). Estimates are ATEs versus control on the original outcome scale. The binary outcome is on the probability scale.

| Column | Type | Specification |
|---|---|------|
| `condition` | factor | Intervention title per `survey/condition_codenames.csv`. |
| `outcome` | string | Outcome variable name per codebook. |
| `ate` | numeric | Predicted ATE, original units. |

### Overview and the human replication reference

Each submission is scored against the same human sample. The human sample is split into two halves by a preregistered random seed (seed 42, set in the setup chunk above). **Human 1** is the reference half every submission is scored against. **Human 2** predicts Human 1 like any submission would, and its scores define the **human replication reference**, which shows how well a fresh human sample of this size reproduces the reference half. This human reference is evaluated in the same way as a Tier-1 synthetic submission. It is a reference, not a ceiling: Human 2's predictions carry the sampling noise of a half sample of this size, so a synthetic submission built on a much larger sample can legitimately score above it, and if that happens it is a result, not an artifact. Two baseline rows — "no effect" and "all positive" — provide references for the metrics without a natural null (see *Cross-team comparison*). Because the split seed for the human sample is an arbitrary choice, we will provide robustness checks across many alternative splits, so that results do not hinge on the seed we happened to select (*Robustness of the scoring pipeline*, below).

Which of the analyses below applies to a given submission follows from its tier (see *Analysis eligibility by tier*). Tier 1 is eligible for all of them, Tiers 2–3 for the estimate-based subset.

### Estimation functions

Every effect size compared below is produced by the same model functions, applied in the same way to the human reference and to each submission. They produce the average treatment effects per intervention for Section 1 and the condition × moderator interactions for Section 2. These functions are unchanged from v1, and their full statistical rationale is in the [human study preregistration](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20160212). We reproduce them here so this document stands alone.

`run_main_treatment_model()` estimates each intervention's ATE against the shared control by OLS with HC2 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and BH-adjusted p-values.


```{.r .cell-code}
print_a_function_from_file("run_main_treatment_model")
```

```r
run_main_treatment_model <- function(data,
                                     outcome,
                                     condition_var = "condition",
                                     covariates    = NULL,
                                     weights       = NULL,
                                     adjust_method = "BH") {
  
  # Formula
  rhs           <- paste(c(condition_var, covariates), collapse = " + ")
  model_formula <- as.formula(paste(outcome, "~", rhs))
  
  # Baseline (control) level
  baseline <- levels(data[[condition_var]])[1]
  
  # Fit
  fit <- lm(
    model_formula,
    data    = data,
    weights = if (!is.null(weights)) data[[weights]] else NULL
  )
  
  # Robust VCOV (HC2)
  vcov_robust <- sandwich::vcovHC(fit, type = "HC2")
  
  results <- lmtest::coeftest(fit, vcov = vcov_robust) |>
    broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(str_detect(term, paste0("^", condition_var))) |>
    mutate(
      outcome          = outcome,
      condition        = str_remove(term, condition_var),
      baseline         = baseline,
      p.value_adjusted = p.adjust(p.value, method = adjust_method), 
      significant_adjusted = case_when(
        p.value_adjusted < .001 ~ "***",
        p.value_adjusted < .01  ~ "**",
        p.value_adjusted < .05  ~ "*",
        TRUE                    ~ NA_character_
      )
    ) |>
    select(-term)
  
  return(results)
}

```

`run_main_treatment_model_binary()` is the counterpart for the binary newsletter-signup outcome. It fits a logistic regression and returns marginal effects on the probability scale.

```r
run_main_treatment_model_binary <- function(data,
                                            outcome,
                                            condition_var = "condition",
                                            covariates    = NULL,
                                            weights       = NULL,
                                            adjust_method = "BH") {
  
  rhs           <- paste(c(condition_var, covariates), collapse = " + ")
  model_formula <- as.formula(paste(outcome, "~", rhs))
  baseline      <- levels(data[[condition_var]])[1]
  
  fit <- glm(
    model_formula,
    data    = data,
    family  = binomial(link = "logit"),
    weights = if (!is.null(weights)) data[[weights]] else NULL
  )
  
  vcov_robust <- sandwich::vcovHC(fit, type = "HC2")
  
  # Log-odds results — for inference
  log_odds <- lmtest::coeftest(fit, vcov = vcov_robust) |>
    broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(str_detect(term, paste0("^", condition_var))) |>
    mutate(
      outcome              = outcome,
      condition            = str_remove(term, condition_var),
      baseline             = baseline,
      p.value_adjusted     = p.adjust(p.value, method = adjust_method),
      significant_adjusted = case_when(
        p.value_adjusted < .001 ~ "***",
        p.value_adjusted < .01  ~ "**",
        p.value_adjusted < .05  ~ "*",
        TRUE                    ~ NA_character_
      ),
      odds_ratio   = exp(estimate),
      or_conf.low  = exp(conf.low),
      or_conf.high = exp(conf.high)
    ) |>
    select(-term)
  
  # Marginal effects — for interpretation (probability scale)
  marginal_effects <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(
    fit,
    variables = condition_var,
    vcov      = vcov_robust,
    newdata = data |> select(all_of(c(outcome, condition_var, covariates)))
  ) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    select(contrast, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
    mutate(
      condition            = str_remove(contrast, " - .+$"),
      outcome              = outcome,
      baseline             = baseline,
      p.value_adjusted     = p.adjust(p.value, method = adjust_method),
      significant_adjusted = case_when(
        p.value_adjusted < .001 ~ "***",
        p.value_adjusted < .01  ~ "**",
        p.value_adjusted < .05  ~ "*",
        TRUE                    ~ NA_character_
      )
    )
  
  list(
    log_odds         = log_odds,
    marginal_effects = marginal_effects
  )
}

```

`run_moderator_model()` estimates the condition × moderator interactions used for the subgroup analysis (Section 2). For the binary newsletter-signup outcome the benchmark's subgroup scoring runs this same OLS function as a linear probability model: in the saturated condition × moderator specification, the OLS interaction coefficient equals the difference-in-differences of the cell signup proportions, in probability units, which convert to percentage points like every other outcome. A logistic model gives the same number: both saturated models fit the cell proportions exactly, so converting the logit back to the probability scale (as `run_main_treatment_model_binary()` does via marginal effects for the ATEs) and taking the second difference reproduces the identical difference-in-differences — we verified this numerically. The linear probability model computes this quantity directly, with valid HC2 standard errors, and it stays defined when a small demographic cell contains no signups at all, a case in which the logit coefficients diverge.


```{.r .cell-code}
print_a_function_from_file("run_moderator_model")
```

```r
run_moderator_model <- function(data,
                                outcome,
                                moderator,
                                condition_var     = "condition",
                                covariates        = NULL,
                                weights           = NULL,
                                adjust_method     = "BH",
                                compute_predicted = TRUE) {
  
  rhs           <- paste(c(paste0(condition_var, " * ", moderator), covariates),
                         collapse = " + ")
  model_formula <- as.formula(paste(outcome, "~", rhs))
  baseline      <- levels(data[[condition_var]])[1]
  
  fit <- lm(
    model_formula,
    data    = data,
    weights = if (!is.null(weights)) data[[weights]] else NULL
  )
  
  vcov_robust <- sandwich::vcovHC(fit, type = "HC2")
  
  interaction_effects <- lmtest::coeftest(fit, vcov = vcov_robust) |>
    broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(str_detect(term, ":")) |>
    mutate(
      baseline             = baseline,
      condition            = str_extract(term, paste0("(?<=", condition_var, ")[^:]+")),
      moderator_level      = str_remove(str_extract(term, "(?<=:).+"), moderator),
      p.value_adjusted     = p.adjust(p.value, method = adjust_method),
      significant_adjusted = case_when(
        p.value_adjusted < .001 ~ "***",
        p.value_adjusted < .01  ~ "**",
        p.value_adjusted < .05  ~ "*",
        TRUE                    ~ NA_character_
      )
    )
  
  is_numeric_mod <- is.numeric(data[[moderator]])

  # `predicted_effects` (marginal effects via marginaleffects) is the expensive
  # part of this function. Callers that only need the interaction coefficients
  # — e.g. the amendment's subgroup leaderboard, which scores estimate-only
  # pairs across many mock teams — can skip it with compute_predicted = FALSE.
  predicted_effects <- NULL

  if (compute_predicted && !is_numeric_mod) {
    predicted_effects <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(
      fit,
      variables = condition_var,
      by        = moderator,
      vcov      = vcov_robust,
      newdata   = "mean"
    ) |>
      as_tibble() |>
      mutate(
        condition            = str_remove(contrast, " - .+$"),
        moderator_level      = .data[[moderator]],
        baseline             = baseline,
        p.value_adjusted     = p.adjust(p.value, method = adjust_method),
        significant_adjusted = case_when(
          p.value_adjusted < .001 ~ "***",
          p.value_adjusted < .01  ~ "**",
          p.value_adjusted < .05  ~ "*",
          TRUE                    ~ NA_character_
        )
      ) |>
      filter(!is.na(condition)) |>
      select(condition, moderator_level, estimate, conf.low, conf.high,
             p.value, p.value_adjusted, significant_adjusted, baseline)
  }

  if (compute_predicted && is_numeric_mod) {
    predicted_effects <- marginaleffects::comparisons(
      fit,
      variables = condition_var,
      vcov      = vcov_robust,
      newdata   = do.call(
        marginaleffects::datagrid,
        c(list(model = fit),
          setNames(list(fivenum(data[[moderator]])), moderator))
      )
    ) |>
      as_tibble() |>
      mutate(
        condition            = str_remove(contrast, " - .+$"),
        moderator_value      = .data[[moderator]],
        baseline             = baseline,
        p.value_adjusted     = p.adjust(p.value, method = adjust_method),
        significant_adjusted = case_when(
          p.value_adjusted < .001 ~ "***",
          p.value_adjusted < .01  ~ "**",
          p.value_adjusted < .05  ~ "*",
          TRUE                    ~ NA_character_
        )
      ) |>
      filter(!is.na(condition)) |>
      select(condition, moderator_value, estimate, conf.low, conf.high,
             p.value, p.value_adjusted, significant_adjusted, baseline)
  }
  
  list(
    interaction_effects = interaction_effects,
    predicted_effects   = predicted_effects
  )
}

```

### Comparison functions

The comparison metrics are implemented by a small set of helper functions, applied symmetrically to the human reference and to each submission.

#### Comparison metrics

The estimate-based metrics compare the point estimates of a submission with those of the human reference, for ATEs (Section 1) and moderator interaction estimates (Section 2). They are reported in increasing order of strictness and implemented in `pooled_metrics()` (shown under *Scoring functions*, below).

- **Directional agreement (%)**. The share of estimates with the same sign as the human estimate. Does the approach at least get the direction of each effect right? A predicted exact zero makes no directional claim and scores half credit — the expected score of a coin flip — which keeps every pair in every submission's denominator. The chance level to read this metric against is *not* 50%: every intervention was designed to increase trust, so if most human effects come out positive, a mindless "every message works" strategy beats 50% without any skill. The empirical chance level is the share of positive human ATEs, reported as the all-positive baseline row in the leaderboard.
- **Spearman $\rho$**. The rank correlation of the point estimates. Does the approach rank the interventions in the same order as humans? It is insensitive to scale or offset, so an approach that inflates all effects equally still scores $\rho$ = 1.
- **Pearson r**. The linear correlation of the point estimates. It captures whether predicted and human effects rise and fall together in proportion, but not whether their absolute size matches.
- **Pearson r within outcomes**. The pooled Pearson r credits two different kinds of knowledge: knowing which *outcomes* are movable at all (attitude sliders shift by a couple of points, donations barely move — generic knowledge available from the literature) and knowing which *messages* work, the skill this benchmark tests. As a companion, we report the correlation computed within outcomes: each outcome's mean effect is subtracted on both sides before correlating, which is the same as adding outcome fixed effects to a regression of human on predicted effects. What survives is message-level skill only, and the gap to the pooled r says how much of the pooled score came from outcome-level knowledge.
- **RMSE**. The root mean squared error, the average size of the prediction errors. In the cross-team analysis every estimate is expressed in **percentage points (pp) of its outcome's scale range** before scoring (see *Scoring principle*, below), so RMSE reads in pp and is reported both pooled across outcomes and per outcome, matching @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a, whose primary archive reports RMSE pooled across experiments in exactly these units. To judge whether an RMSE is good, compare it to the standard deviation of the human ATEs — how much the 16 human effects spread out around their mean (a spread across interventions, not a standard error). A submission that ignores the interventions entirely and predicts the same value for all of them can at best reach an RMSE equal to that SD, by predicting the mean ATE. A submission with intervention-specific skill must therefore come in below it. (In v1, which scores each outcome on its own raw scale, RMSE stays per outcome and is omitted from the pooled row.)

#### Adjusted correlation and RMSE (noise-corrected)

The effects in the human sample are noisy. That noise mechanically drags the correlation between effects of the human and synthetic sample down, because it inflates the observed spread of the reference effects. The raw Pearson r divides by that inflated spread and is biased toward zero. The same noise inflates the RMSE.

Wherever Pearson r appears in the cross-team analysis we therefore report, beside the raw value, a noise-corrected correlation **r~adj~** and a noise-corrected RMSE (`adjusted_metrics()`). The correction works by subtraction. Because the sampling noise is independent (that's an assumption we make), the true spread of the reference effects is their observed spread minus the average known sampling variance. The adjusted correlation divides the covariance by that corrected spread (Spearman disattenuation with known error variances). This method is similar to the meta-analytic r~adj~ of @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a, but uses fewer assumptions. As @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a, we will report r and r~adj~ side by side in the manuscript. This allows us to directly compare our results to their larger megastudy archive, the closest analogue to this benchmark^[We take Ashokkumar et al.'s megastudy figures, not their headline r = .85, as the reference because the two numbers measure different tasks. The .85 is a correlation over 469 effects pooled from 70 unrelated survey experiments, spanning many topics, treatments, and outcomes. Their megastudy figures instead measure how well the model distinguishes the several interventions of a single megastudy against that study's shared control, which is exactly this benchmark's setting (16 interventions, one control). Ashokkumar et al. report the megastudies as a separate secondary archive (15 megastudies, 606 effects) and note that these correlations are lower than the primary archive's.], survey experiments reach r = .43 (r~adj~ = .52) and text-based treatments r = .45 (r~adj~ = .54).

The adjusted RMSE applies the same logic to the RMSE. It subtracts the average reference sampling variance from the average squared prediction error and takes the square root. When a submission's errors are smaller than the reference sampling variance, the subtraction goes negative; the adjusted RMSE is then reported as 0 with a flag, meaning the submission's errors are at or below the sampling noise of the human reference estimates — indistinguishable from perfect at this reference precision. The same rule applies inside every bootstrap replicate (an NA would drop exactly the best replicates from the interval).


```{.r .cell-code}
print_a_function_from_file("adjusted_metrics")
```

```r
adjusted_metrics <- function(pairs) {
  ok <- pairs |> filter(!is.na(estimate_h), !is.na(estimate_l), !is.na(se_h))

  if (nrow(ok) < 3) return(tibble(pearson_adj = NA_real_, rmse_adj = NA_real_,
                                  rmse_adj_at_floor = NA))

  var_true <- var(ok$estimate_h) - mean(ok$se_h^2)
  mse_true <- mean((ok$estimate_h - ok$estimate_l)^2) - mean(ok$se_h^2)

  tibble(
    pearson_adj = if (var_true > 0 && sd(ok$estimate_l) > 0)
      max(-1, min(1, cov(ok$estimate_l, ok$estimate_h) /
                       (sd(ok$estimate_l) * sqrt(var_true))))
      else NA_real_,
    rmse_adj          = sqrt(max(mse_true, 0)),
    rmse_adj_at_floor = mse_true <= 0
  )
}

```

#### Distribution comparison metrics

`compare_distributions()` compares response distributions for a single condition and outcome using four metrics:

- **Variance ratio** (submission variance / human variance). It captures only relative spread. A ratio of 1 means equal spread and says nothing about shape. A ratio below 1 means the synthetic responses vary less than the human ones, the most widely reported problem with synthetic samples.
- **OVL (overlapping coefficient)**. The share of area the two kernel density estimates have in common (1 = identical distributions, 0 = no overlap). It summarizes overall shape similarity.
- **KS D-statistic**. The largest gap between the two empirical cumulative distributions (0 = indistinguishable everywhere). It is sensitive to local departures that OVL might average away.
- **Wasserstein-1 distance (W1)**, enabled with `include_w1 = TRUE` (new in this preregistration, not part of v1). The area between the two cumulative distributions, in outcome scale points (0 = identical). It is the bandwidth-free companion to OVL: kernel density estimates depend on bandwidths, which change with sample size and leak density past the 0/100 scale bounds, while W1 has no tuning parameter.

In the benchmark, the OVL and W1 evaluation grid is fixed to each outcome's full scale range (0–100 for the sliders, $0–10 for the donation), so every submission is scored on the identical grid (changelog item 26). With the default empirical grid — the observed minimum-to-maximum of the two samples, kept for v1 compatibility — the integration range would follow each submission's own responses, and the resulting areas would not be comparable across teams.


```{.r .cell-code}
print_a_function_from_file("compare_distributions")
```

```r
compare_distributions <- function(human_data, llm_data, outcome, condition_val,
                                  include_w1 = FALSE, range = NULL) {
  x <- human_data |> filter(condition == condition_val) |> pull(all_of(outcome)) |> na.omit()
  y <- llm_data   |> filter(condition == condition_val) |> pull(all_of(outcome)) |> na.omit()
  fr <- if (is.null(range)) NULL else range[1]
  to <- if (is.null(range)) NULL else range[2]
  out <- tibble(
    condition      = as.character(condition_val),
    ovl            = compute_ovl(x, y, from = fr, to = to),
    ks_d           = suppressWarnings(ks.test(x, y)$statistic),
    variance_ratio = var(y) / var(x)  # > 1: clones more variable; < 1: less variable
  )
  if (include_w1) out <- out |> mutate(w1 = compute_w1(x, y, from = fr, to = to), .after = ovl)
  out
}

```

```r
compute_ovl <- function(x, y, n_grid = 512, from = NULL, to = NULL) {
  lo <- if (is.null(from)) min(c(x, y)) else from
  hi <- if (is.null(to))   max(c(x, y)) else to
  if (lo == hi) return(NA_real_)
  # Evaluate both KDEs on the same grid, then integrate the overlap area
  d_h <- density(x, from = lo, to = hi, n = n_grid)
  d_l <- density(y, from = lo, to = hi, n = n_grid)
  sum(pmin(d_h$y, d_l$y)) * (hi - lo) / n_grid
}

```


```{.r .cell-code}
print_a_function_from_file("compute_w1")
```

```r
compute_w1 <- function(x, y, n_grid = 512, from = NULL, to = NULL) {
  lo <- if (is.null(from)) min(c(x, y)) else from
  hi <- if (is.null(to))   max(c(x, y)) else to
  if (lo == hi) return(0)
  gr <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = n_grid)
  mean(abs(ecdf(x)(gr) - ecdf(y)(gr))) * (hi - lo)
}

```

#### Calibration regression

Correlation tells us only whether the human and predicted effects covary. It does not capture baseline differences or scaling. An approach could inflate every effect by a factor of two and still score Pearson r = 1. The calibration regression captures this.

`run_calibration_pooled()` regresses human ATEs on predicted ATEs, $\mathrm{ATE}_{human} = \alpha + \beta \times \mathrm{ATE}_{predicted}$, across all condition × outcome pairs pooled over the 13 outcomes (16 × 13 = 208 points, every estimate in pp of scale range). The slope $\beta$ captures proportional scaling ($\beta = 1$ is perfect), the intercept $\alpha$ a constant offset added to all effects ($\alpha = 0$ is perfect). An approach can be perfectly proportional and still be off by the same amount on every prediction: if the clones react to receiving any message at all with the same extra shift, one that humans do not show, every predicted ATE is too large by that fixed amount and the regression returns $\beta = 1$ with a negative $\alpha$. We report $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with 95% intervals and read them descriptively (following @ashokkumarLargeLanguageModels2026a). We do not test the point hypotheses $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 1$, and instead report the slope with an interval and interpret its size. The intervals come from the intervention cluster bootstrap, the same resampling (identical seed and draws) that produces every other uncertainty interval in the cross-team analysis (see *Uncertainty intervals on the leaderboard*): the 13 outcomes within an intervention share that intervention's draw, and resampling interventions whole respects that dependence, where heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors would treat the 208 points as independent.

A slope below 1 has two possible readings, and only one of them is the approach's fault. The first is genuine exaggeration: the approach systematically predicts larger effects than humans show. The second is sampling noise in the predictions themselves. Noise in the *human* effects never biases the slope (it only widens the residuals), but noise in the *predicted* effects drags the slope toward zero by the reliability of the predictions, $\lambda = 1 - \overline{se_{pred}^2} / \mathrm{var}(\mathrm{ATE}_{predicted})$. A perfectly calibrated Tier-1 entry built on a synthetic sample near the precision floor can therefore print a raw $\beta$ well below 1 without exaggerating anything — and by an amount that depends on its sample size, so the raw slope would partly rank simulation budgets. For Tier-1 entries, whose effects we refit ourselves so their standard errors are known, we therefore report a corrected slope beside the raw one: $\beta_{adj} = \beta / \hat{\lambda}$, the slope of the entry's latent (infinite-sample) predictions. The raw $\beta$ stays the reported, Ashokkumar-comparable quantity — it is also the right shrinkage factor for using an entry's numbers as delivered — while $\beta_{adj}$ answers whether the *approach* exaggerates. Tiers 2–3 submit point predictions with no standard errors, so no correction exists there and a $\beta$ below 1 is read as exaggeration, prediction noise, or both. This mirrors how the noise in the reference is handled for the correlation (r beside r~adj~): the raw value stays comparable, the corrected value carries the interpretation. Correcting $\beta$ takes nothing away from the noise penalty a small synthetic sample rightly pays — that penalty lives in r, RMSE, and the other scored metrics, while $\beta$'s job is to name the *kind* of error.


```{.r .cell-code}
print_a_function_from_file("run_calibration_pooled")
```

```r
run_calibration_pooled <- function(pairs) {
  fit <- lm(estimate_h ~ estimate_l, data = pairs)
  cf  <- coef(fit)

  lambda <- if ("se_l" %in% names(pairs) && any(!is.na(pairs$se_l)))
    1 - mean(pairs$se_l^2, na.rm = TRUE) / var(pairs$estimate_l, na.rm = TRUE)
  else NA_real_

  tibble(
    alpha    = unname(cf[1]),
    beta     = unname(cf[2]),
    beta_adj = if (!is.na(lambda) && lambda > 0) unname(cf[2]) / lambda
               else NA_real_
  )
}

```

#### Demographic baseline and predictability metrics

`compare_demographic_baselines()` computes, for each moderator, the RMSE between human and synthetic sample cell means in the control condition. (The function also returns a per-moderator Pearson correlation, kept for v1 compatibility, which the benchmark does not report: the moderators have three to seven groups, a correlation over so few points is unstable — over two points it is always exactly ±1 — and correlation ignores level and scale, the two things baseline calibration is about. See changelog item 23.) `compare_demographic_predictability()` fits separate OLS regressions of the outcome on each moderator plus condition fixed effects, returning $R^2$ and dummy-coded coefficients for humans and for the submission. `demographic_parity_gap()` quantifies, for each moderator, the gap between the worst- and best-served demographic group in the control condition. For example, if an approach's control-condition baseline is off by 6 pp for Republicans but only 1 pp for Democrats, the parity gap for partisan identity is 5 pp, with Republicans the worst-served group. Groups under 30 respondents on either side are skipped, and the skipped groups are named, with their sizes, wherever the parity gap is reported (see *Section 3*).


```{.r .cell-code}
print_a_function_from_file("compare_demographic_baselines")
```

```r
compare_demographic_baselines <- function(human_data, llm_data,
                                           outcome,
                                           moderators,
                                           condition_var = "condition",
                                           min_cells_r = 0) {
  control_val <- levels(human_data[[condition_var]])[1]

  map_dfr(moderators, function(mod) {
    h_cells <- human_data |>
      filter(.data[[condition_var]] == control_val) |>
      group_by(cell = .data[[mod]]) |>
      summarise(mean_h = mean(.data[[outcome]], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

    l_cells <- llm_data |>
      filter(.data[[condition_var]] == control_val) |>
      group_by(cell = .data[[mod]]) |>
      summarise(mean_l = mean(.data[[outcome]], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

    inner_join(h_cells, l_cells, by = "cell") |>
      summarise(
        moderator = mod,
        r         = if (n() >= min_cells_r)
          cor(mean_h, mean_l, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") else NA_real_,
        rmse      = sqrt(mean((mean_h - mean_l)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
        n_cells   = n()
      )
  })
}

```

```r
compare_demographic_predictability <- function(human_data, llm_data,
                                                outcome,
                                                predictors,
                                                condition_var = "condition") {
  results <- map(predictors, function(mod) {
    formula <- as.formula(paste(outcome, "~", mod, "+", condition_var))
    fit_h   <- lm(formula, data = human_data)
    fit_l   <- lm(formula, data = llm_data)

    rsq <- tibble(
      moderator = mod,
      source    = c("human", "llm"),
      r_squared = c(broom::glance(fit_h)$r.squared, broom::glance(fit_l)$r.squared)
    )

    coefs_h <- broom::tidy(fit_h, conf.int = TRUE) |>
      filter(str_detect(term, fixed(mod))) |>
      select(term, est_h = estimate, lo_h = conf.low, hi_h = conf.high)

    coefs_l <- broom::tidy(fit_l, conf.int = TRUE) |>
      filter(str_detect(term, fixed(mod))) |>
      select(term, est_l = estimate, lo_l = conf.low, hi_l = conf.high)

    coefs <- inner_join(coefs_h, coefs_l, by = "term") |>
      mutate(moderator = mod)

    list(r_squared = rsq, coefficients = coefs)
  })

  list(
    r_squared    = map_dfr(results, "r_squared"),
    coefficients = map_dfr(results, "coefficients")
  )
}

```
